sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses the abuse of older people, disabled people and children, and deaths in nursing homes. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Nursing homes are not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track nursing homes or assisted living facilities.

But the two follow the same business model: keep the beds full and the staff thin. The people in the beds depend on that staff for their care. Someone has to pay for it. Some of the same companies and investors have owned both, often at the same time. One hospital chain ran nursing homes and psychiatric hospitals for teenagers in the 1980s. Private equity firms have bought nursing home chains and teen treatment companies. A nursing home landlord owns a children's psychiatric hospital. Both industries grew out of the almshouses, where old, disabled and poor people and children were once held together ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/), [how the threads met](/birth-of-the-tti/)).

We are not experts on long-term care. Residents, their families, ombudsmen and the organizations listed below have done this work for decades.

sections.label: The same owners
sections.heading: The same owners
sections.body:
The same owners have run both, often at the same time.

Table: Owners of nursing homes and youth programs
| Owner | Nursing homes and assisted living | Youth programs |
|---|---|---|
| National Medical Enterprises (later Tenet) | Hillhaven, bought in 1979; 287 long-term care facilities by 1994[^1][^2] | Psychiatric Institutes of America, bought in 1983: 73 hospitals by 1991 that admitted children and teenagers. Its operating company pleaded guilty in 1994 to paying illegal remuneration[^1][^3][^2] |
| The Carlyle Group | HCR ManorCare, over 500 nursing and assisted living centers, from 2007 until its 2018 bankruptcy[^4][^5][^6] | Newport Academy, ages 12 to 22, 2017 to 2021[^7] ([company page](/operator/newport-healthcare/)) |
| Onex | Skilled Healthcare Group, 96 nursing and assisted living facilities by 2008; owned 2005 to 2015[^8][^9][^10] | Res-Care, from 2004, with about 2,000 "at-risk and troubled youths" in juvenile programs in 2003; renamed BrightSpring in 2018[^11][^12][^13][^14]. Newport Healthcare, from 2021[^15] |
| Bain Capital | Estia Health, aged care homes in Australia, from 2023[^16]. Through Broadstep: Good Hope Manor assisted living in Milwaukee, from January 2021[^17] | Aspen Education Group, through CRC Health, from 2006[^18] ([company page](/operator/aspen-education-group/)). Through Broadstep: Excalibur Youth Services' six treatment facilities in South Carolina, bought the same month[^19] |
| Sabra Health Care REIT (owns the buildings) | Hundreds of skilled nursing buildings[^20] | Since 2017, six Aurora psychiatric hospitals with "child and adolescent psychiatric care," among them [Chicago Lakeshore Hospital](/facility/chicago-lakeshore-hospital-il/)[^21][^20] |

Two West Virginia programs under the ResCare name are in our records.

sections.label: What thin staffing costs
sections.heading: What thin staffing costs
sections.body:
Thin staffing is where the money comes from, and someone has to pay for it. After private equity bought nursing homes, patient deaths rose 11 percent: about 22,500 more deaths over twelve years. The researchers blamed "declines in measures of patient well-being, nurse staffing, and compliance with care standards."[^22]

In 2024 the federal government set the first minimum staffing for nursing homes. Only 11 percent of for-profit homes met it, against 41 percent of nonprofits.[^23] In 2025 two federal courts struck it down. Congress barred enforcing it until 2034, and the Medicare agency repealed it.[^24]

Youth program owners say it out loud. "You can make money in this business if you control staffing," Jay Ripley, a co-founder of [Sequel Youth and Family Services](/operator/sequel-tsi/), told business students in 2015. The Senate Finance Committee quoted him in 2024. Understaffing, it concluded, is "a cornerstone of the RTF business model."[^25]

Table: What happens to nursing home residents
| What was found | Figure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Staff who say they abused a resident in the past year | 2 in 3 | [^26] |
| Abuse citations against nursing homes, 2013 to 2017 | More than doubled, from 430 to 875 | [^27] |
| Residents' emergency room visits caused by possible abuse or neglect (2016) | 1 in 5 | [^28] |
| Of those, cases the nursing home did not report to the state | 84 percent | [^28] |
| Medicare residents harmed by their care in a nursing home stay (2011) | 22 percent; 59 percent of the harm preventable | [^29] |
| Residents whose care contributed to their deaths, in a single month (2011, projected) | 1,538 | [^29] |

sections.label: The same drugs
sections.heading: The same drugs
sections.body:
Both drug the people in their care to make them easier to manage. In March 2026 the federal Office of Inspector General found that nursing homes "inappropriately diagnosed residents with schizophrenia to mask the misuse of antipsychotic drugs."[^30] Human Rights Watch counted "more than 179,000 people, mostly older and living with dementia," given antipsychotics every week without an approved diagnosis. Using the drugs "for staff convenience or to discipline or punish a resident" can be abuse, it noted.[^31]

The Senate found the same in youth residential treatment. All four companies it investigated use chemical restraint, "the most restrictive type of restraint." Children in their care are often on five or more medications at once.[^32]

To the companies that own them, a woman with dementia in a nursing home and a fifteen-year-old in a treatment center are the same thing: a bed to keep full, with as few staff as possible to look after the person in it.

If you know of another company or investor that has owned both nursing homes and youth programs, please [tell us](/contact/).

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911.
- **Long-Term Care Ombudsman.** Every state has one. Ombudsmen take complaints from nursing home and assisted living residents and their families, and work for the resident. Find yours through the Eldercare Locator, 1-800-677-1116, or [Consumer Voice's directory](https://theconsumervoice.org/get-help/).
- **State survey agency.** Complaints about abuse, neglect, too few staff or unsafe conditions in a nursing home go to the state survey agency, usually part of the state health department. CMS lists [each state's agency](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/quality-safety-oversight-general-information/contact-information), or call 1-800-MEDICARE, 1-800-633-4227 (TTY 1-877-486-2048), for the contact.
- **Adult Protective Services** takes reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of older and disabled adults. Find your state's number through [NAPSA](https://www.napsa-now.org/help-in-your-area/).
- **Medicaid Fraud Control Units** investigate and prosecute [abuse and neglect of residents](https://oig.hhs.gov/fraud/medicaid-fraud-control-units-mfcu/) in facilities that take Medicaid.
- **Protection and Advocacy.** For disabled residents, including younger people who want to leave a nursing home, there is a [Protection and Advocacy agency](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/) in every state and territory.
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

For abuse in a youth program, see [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care](https://theconsumervoice.org/): Founded in 1975 as the National Citizens' Coalition for Nursing Home Reform; speaks for long-term care residents nationally and runs the National Long-Term Care Ombudsman Resource Center.
- [Long Term Care Community Coalition (nursinghome411)](https://nursinghome411.org/): Publishes nursing home staffing, inspection and antipsychotic data and guides for residents and families.
- [Center for Medicare Advocacy](https://medicareadvocacy.org/): A nonprofit law organization; tracks nursing home enforcement and residents' rights.
- [Justice in Aging](https://justiceinaging.org/): Legal advocacy for older adults with low incomes, including the rights of people living in nursing homes.
- [California Advocates for Nursing Home Reform](https://canhr.org/): Fact sheets, legal referrals and advocacy for people in California's long-term care facilities.
- [ADAPT](https://adapt.org/): A disability rights group, led by disabled people, that fights for the right to live at home instead of in nursing homes.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you live or work in long-term care, or have a family member who does, and something here is wrong or missing, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.
